framework: Asking the Right Questions: A Guide to Critical Thinking
key_work: Asking the Right Questions: A Guide to Critical Thinking (1st ed. 1981, 12th ed. 2019)
description: Browne and Keeley's framework consists of 10 sequential questions that form a complete protocol for analyzing any argument or persuasive text. The genius of the framework is its sequenced diagnostic logic: each question reveals a different potential failure mode, and applying all 10 ensures comprehensive critical analysis.
dewey_connection: The Browne-Keeley sequence maps directly to Dewey's reflective thinking: beginning with framing (questions 1-2), proceeding through analysis (3-8), and arriving at integrative judgment (9-10). The emphasis on 'right questions' echoes Dewey's insistence that the quality of inquiry depends on the quality of the questions it addresses.
paul_elder_connection: Questions 1-2 map to Purpose and Question-at-Issue; 3-5 to Concepts and Assumptions; 6-7 to Information and Inference; 8-10 to Implications and Point of View.

ten_questions.question: What are the issue and the conclusion?
ten_questions.purpose: Identify the focal point of the argument before any evaluation can proceed. Without clear identification of the conclusion, analysis has no target.

issue_types.description: Concerns what is, was, or will be true — empirically resolvable in principle
Concerns what should be, what is right, what is valuable — requires value judgments

diagnostic_questions: What is the author trying to persuade me to believe or do?
If I was to summarize this argument in one sentence, what would I say?
Is this issue descriptive or prescriptive?
failure_modes: Confusing the issue with the conclusion
Failing to distinguish prescriptive from descriptive claims

ten_questions.question: What are the reasons?
ten_questions.purpose: Identify the explicit and implicit reasons (premises) offered in support of the conclusion. Reasons are what the author wants us to accept as grounds for accepting the conclusion.
diagnostic_questions: Why should I believe this conclusion?
What reasons are explicitly stated?
Are there unstated reasons being assumed?
Can I map the reasoning: 'Because of [reasons], therefore [conclusion]'?
failure_modes: Accepting conclusions without identifying the reasons
Treating repetition of conclusion as a reason

ten_questions.question: Which words or phrases are ambiguous?
ten_questions.purpose: Identify key terms whose vagueness or ambiguity could mask a weak argument or generate false agreement. Different definitions of a key term may make the argument succeed or fail.
diagnostic_questions: What are the key terms in the issue and reasons?
Could any of these terms be interpreted in multiple ways?
Which interpretation makes the argument strongest? Which weakest?
Is the term used consistently throughout the argument?
failure_modes: Equivocation — using a term in two different senses
Emotive language smuggling in value judgments as factual claims

ten_questions.question: What are the value conflicts and assumptions?
ten_questions.purpose: Identify the value assumptions — beliefs about desirable ends and standards of conduct — that the author must hold for the reasoning to proceed. Value assumptions are especially important in prescriptive arguments.
diagnostic_questions: What values does this reasoning implicitly prioritize?
If this conclusion is true, what must the author value?
What are the competing values that someone who disagrees would hold?
Is there an implicit ranking of values embedded in the argument?
failure_modes: Treating one's own value assumptions as universal
Failing to make value conflicts explicit
Disguising prescriptive claims as empirical ones

ten_questions.question: What are the descriptive assumptions?
ten_questions.purpose: Identify the factual assumptions — beliefs about how the world is — that the author takes for granted. Descriptive assumptions are unstated premises treated as obvious but that may be contested.
diagnostic_questions: What must be true for this reason to support this conclusion?
What am I being asked to take on faith?
Are the reasons relevant to the conclusion only if something else is also true?
What implicit beliefs about people, institutions, or causation does this argument depend on?
failure_modes: Accepting background assumptions as obviously true
Failing to distinguish assumptions from established facts
Missing the hidden premises that do the work

ten_questions.question: Are there any fallacies in the reasoning?
ten_questions.purpose: Identify formal and informal fallacies — errors in the logical structure of the reasoning that are disguised as valid arguments.

key_fallacies.description: Attacking the person making the argument rather than the argument itself
Assuming that one event will inevitably lead to a chain of negative events without justification
Citing sources that lack relevant expertise, have conflicts of interest, or are not representative of expert consensus
Presenting only two options when more exist
Using the conclusion (in disguised form) as one of the premises
Misrepresenting an opponent's position to make it easier to attack
Substituting emotional manipulation for logical support

diagnostic_questions: Does the reasoning make illegitimate shortcuts?
Is the author attacking persons rather than arguments?
Is the authority cited relevant and unbiased?
Has the opposing view been accurately represented?

ten_questions.question: How good is the evidence?
ten_questions.purpose: Evaluate the quality of the empirical evidence used to support factual claims. Even valid reasoning fails if the evidence is poor.

evaluation_criteria: Is the analogy being used to prove or illustrate?

diagnostic_questions: What type of evidence is being offered?
Is this the best type of evidence for this claim?
What are the limitations of this evidence?
Could this evidence be interpreted differently?

ten_questions.question: Are there rival causes?
ten_questions.purpose: Determine whether alternative explanations for the evidence exist that would undermine the causal claims of the argument. Correlation does not establish causation.
rival_cause_types: Reverse causation — Y causes X rather than X causes Y
Confounding variable — Z causes both X and Y
Placebo effect — expectation produces the outcome, not the intervention
Post hoc ergo propter hoc — temporal precedence confused with causation
Selection bias — the groups being compared differ in relevant ways
diagnostic_questions: Could this correlation be explained by a third variable?
Could the direction of causation be reversed?
What would a skeptic say is the real explanation for this data?
Has the author controlled for alternative explanations?

ten_questions.question: Are the statistics deceptive?
ten_questions.purpose: Identify ways in which numerical data can mislead even when technically accurate — through selective presentation, inappropriate comparison groups, or misleading framing.

common_deceptions.example: 'Our drug reduces mortality by 50%!' — from 2% to 1% (relative risk vs. absolute risk)
Using mean income when distribution is highly skewed; median tells a different story
'Crime increased 100%!' — from 1 case to 2 cases in a small town
'Interest rates increased 50%' — from 2% to 3% is a 50% increase but only 1 percentage point
Voluntary online surveys over-represent people with strong opinions

diagnostic_questions: What is the base rate being compared against?
What measures of central tendency would show a different picture?
Who is included and excluded from the statistics?
Are these relative or absolute numbers?

ten_questions.question: What significant information is omitted?
ten_questions.purpose: Identify what the argument does NOT say that would significantly affect one's evaluation of it. All arguments present a selected slice of available information; what is left out is as important as what is included.
omission_types: Long-term consequences of the proposed policy
Relevant context that would reframe the issue
The funding source or interests of those making the argument
diagnostic_questions: What would someone who disagrees want me to know that this argument doesn't mention?
What are the costs, risks, or downsides of the proposed conclusion?
What context would change how I evaluate this argument?
If the argument is correct, what else should be true that I could check?

application_protocol.description: The 10 questions are designed to be applied sequentially — each question builds on the previous. Stopping at question 3 without completing the sequence produces an incomplete analysis.

quick_version.description: When time is limited, questions 1, 2, 5, 6, and 10 provide the highest-leverage analysis.
quick_version.rationale: Issue/conclusion, reasons, descriptive assumptions, fallacies, and omitted information cover the most common argument failure modes.

application_protocol.strong_version: Apply all 10 questions in sequence to produce a comprehensive argument evaluation.

app_usage.template_feature: 10 questions as a template for structured argument analysis
app_usage.exercise_feature: Each question generates a distinct exercise type
app_usage.quick_reference: Question bank surfaced during argument evaluation tasks
app_usage.llm_integration: Claude can evaluate user arguments against the 10-question rubric
